questions.q: What is Meridian Fulfillment Co., as used in this lesson?
options: A fictional, illustrative company invented for this lesson to demonstrate how the course's concepts fit together
A real logistics company whose governance program is documented as a verified case study
An anonymized version of a real company whose name has been changed
A composite average of several real companies' governance programs
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly labels Meridian Fulfillment Co. as fictional and illustrative — it is not a real company or a real case study, only a teaching device.

questions.q: In the walkthrough, why is Meridian's wrong-address problem described as having a governance root cause rather than being purely a data quality issue?
options: Three different systems each hold a customer address field and nobody has been assigned ownership of which one is authoritative
The e-commerce platform has a software bug that corrupts address fields
Customers are entering their addresses incorrectly at checkout
The warehouse management system lacks the storage capacity for address data
questions.explain: The data quality symptom (wrong addresses) traces back to a governance gap: no owner has declared which of the three systems holds the authoritative record.

questions.q: Why does the walkthrough choose a federated-leaning operating model rather than a fully centralized governance office for Meridian?
options: It fits a few-hundred-person company with one concrete problem — centralized enough to pick an authoritative source, federated enough to keep local stewardship
Federated models are always required by data protection regulations
A fully centralized model would be cheaper to implement
Meridian has no executive sponsor, so centralization is not possible
questions.explain: The lesson reasons from company size and the scope of the actual problem to a lightweight, federated-leaning model rather than defaulting to the most elaborate option available.

questions.q: In the Chapter 5 sequence applied to Meridian, what determines whether the pilot's approach gets scaled to a second domain?
options: Whether the measured result (address-related complaints) actually dropped against the baseline captured before the pilot began
Whether the executive sponsor personally approves of the pilot's style
Whether exactly ninety days have elapsed, regardless of outcome
Whether a new regulation has been introduced during the pilot window
questions.explain: The scale-or-stop decision from Lesson 27 is applied here: the baseline-vs-result comparison on complaint volume is what decides whether the same sequence repeats for a new domain.

questions.q: According to this lesson's closing note, which course comes next in the Data Governance career path?
options: Data Quality Management
Cloud Data Governance: Azure and AWS
Data Governance Architecture
AI and Machine Learning Governance
questions.explain: The lesson's outro points to Data Quality Management as the next course, picking up the quality side of the governance-vs-management-vs-quality distinction introduced in Lesson 3.
